A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AxProverBase, and their complete text, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison. Retained material can be matched despite substantial reformatting and appendix reordering.

before.justification: v1 reports original component ablations, foundation-model comparisons, and AxProverBase evaluations on PutnamBench, FATE, and LeanCat in Figures 2–3 and Table 1.

after.justification: v3 retains those original evaluations and adds analyses of generated proof traces, error distributions, and token consumption in Appendices C, E, and F.

M1.justification: The proposer, compiler/reviewer, memory alternatives, search tools, and iterative procedure remain unchanged. Appendix B retains the operational prompt content. Expanded descriptions of deterministic verification checks and prompt assembly do not establish a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate PutnamBench, FATE-M/H/X, and LeanCat, using the same 100 PutnamBench problems for ablations. Appendix C illustrates an already evaluated FATE-M problem. SorryDB is newly cited but not evaluated, and formal-only LeanCat input is newly disclosed rather than established as changed coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 replaces the Gemini 3 Pro LeanCat comparator with Claude Opus 4.5 and adds LeanCat comparisons with DeepSeek-Prover-V2, Goedel-Prover-V2, and Kimina-Prover. Appendix F adds Qwen3 and DeepSeek-R1 to FATE cost comparisons. The directly evaluated Hilbert reference in v1's Figure 2 and Section 4.1 is removed, while v3 adds comparisons using externally reported Hilbert results.

E3.justification: Appendices E–F introduce substantial analysis protocols: classifying the first error from each failed attempt and evaluating success against maximum and average token budgets with input/output accounting. FATE comparator token costs are reconstructed from response length and pass counts. The original model configurations, iteration budgets, and ablation sample set remain; these additions do not establish rerunning the retained experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component and thinking-budget ablations, v3 adds error analyses across architectures and foundation models, extensive cost-performance analyses across all evaluated datasets, and a complete two-iteration FATE-M case study. These investigate failure mechanisms and resource efficiency that v1 discussed mainly qualitatively.

E5.justification: The existing confidence intervals, standard errors, 50 independent single-shot samples, and two/three iterative runs are retained. Table 4 newly reports standard deviations across problems for output-token fractions. This adds variability reporting without establishing additional runs or seeds.

E6.justification: AxProverBase's Table 1 success rates remain 54.7%, 98.0%, 66.0%, 24.0%, and 59.0%. v3 adds comparator results, detailed error distributions, and token-budget findings, including 53% fewer name errors and 1.4 million average tokens per PutnamBench problem. The original Hilbert subset result and Gemini 3 Pro LeanCat entry disappear; the new comparisons are not same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: Appendix C newly includes an algebraic derivation and complete Lean proof of FATE-M problem 116: both squared sum and squared difference equal a²+b² when ab=-ba in a ring. This is a limited worked-proof addition, without new theoretical guarantees for the agent.

C1.justification: The minimal-agent contribution and the claimed importance ordering of feedback, memory, and tools remain. v3 recasts memory's stated benefit from preventing cycles to reducing Lean errors, and replaces the discussion's runtime advantage over Hilbert with a claim of similar full-benchmark pass@1 performance at substantially lower token budgets.

C2.justification: v3 substantially develops the mechanism interpretation: better memory, tools, and models reduce low-level Lean errors, allowing more effort on unresolved proof goals. Its new Impact Statement also distinguishes formal proof validity from faithful representation of scientific claims and discusses misformalization, benchmark overfitting, and overreliance. These extend v1's shorter cycle-avoidance and import-error explanations.

D1.justification: v3 clarifies prompt composition, deterministic reviewer checks, monetary-cost normalization, and the exclusion of natural-language descriptions from LeanCat inputs. Appendix C provides actual tool outputs, compiler feedback, memory content, and reviewer exchanges. The existing prompt templates, main hyperparameters, ablation identifiers, and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds SorryDB and Qwen3 references, removes the DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5 reference, and explicitly identifies Ax-Prover as an inspiration. Related-work descriptions of self-play, DeepSeek, Goedel, and Hilbert are revised, while the overall positioning as a minimal general-purpose-model baseline remains.

P1.justification: Section 5 is extensively rewritten, and related-work and experimental explanations are substantially revised, including clearer distinctions between refinement iterations and independent pass@k runs. The appendices are reorganized, prompt instructions receive explanatory introductions, and an Impact Statement is added.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column layout to a two-column conference format. Figure 1 moves to the first page, Figure 2 loses the Hilbert reference line, and Table 1 gains a multi-entry structure. Five new analytical figures and a token-statistics table are added; the retained leaderboard and ablation list are relocated.

improvement.justification: The error breakdowns, token accounting, worked proof trace, and explicit formalization limitation make the retained findings more interpretable and auditable. The added efficiency evidence remains limited by comparisons across separately reported systems and an internal inconsistency: Hilbert pass@1 is 45.9% in Section 2.1 but 55.9% in Table 1 and Appendix F. Overall, v3 provides useful supporting improvements while retaining the core results and some comparative-evaluation weaknesses.
